a: lovemaking
p: The same consonants can be read 'lovemaking' or 'breasts'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex), pointed dodim
readings.en: your lovemaking
readings.plain: lovemaking

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete, 'your breasts are better than wine'); the Latin Vulgate also has 'breasts' (ubera); the same Greek at 1:4 and 4:10
readings.en: your breasts
readings.plain: breasts

why: The consonants are the same; only the vowels differ. The Hebrew dod, 'love, lovemaking', is used for love in the Song and elsewhere (1:4; 4:10; 5:1; 7:12; Proverbs 7:18), while dad, 'breast', is rare (Proverbs 5:19; Ezekiel 23:3). The Masoretic pointing is the old tradition of reading, and the address to a male lover ('your') suits 'lovemaking' better.
b: The Greek translators worked from unpointed Hebrew and wrote 'breasts' at 1:2, 1:4 and 4:10 (Swete's Vaticanus). Some modern scholars take 'breasts' seriously because Proverbs 5:19 uses the related word in praise of a wife. But the same Hebrew in 4:10 is addressed to a woman and cannot mean her lover's breasts without strain, and the plural dodim is the Song's usual word for love-making. The Plain English Translation follows the pointed Hebrew in all three places.

a: The smell of your oils is good,
p: 6Q6, as transcribed, has 'oils' without 'your' and a different form of 'poured out'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.en: your oils are good; oil poured out
readings.plain: The smell of your oils is good,

readings.w: 6Q6 (6QCant), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook; the word between the two phrases is restored
readings.en: good oils … poured out (a different form of the verb)
readings.plain: (good oils … poured out)

why: The differences are slight and do not change the sense. The Masoretic text is complete and the scroll is broken here, so the Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic text.
b: The transcription marks 'oils' and 'poured out' as visible and different from the Masoretic text. The editor of 6Q6 is Baillet (DJD III). I describe only what the transcription shows.

a: We will remember your lovemaking more than wine
p: The Greek has 'we will love your breasts' in 1:4, as in 1:2.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.en: we will remember your lovemaking more than wine
readings.plain: We will remember your lovemaking more than wine

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete); Latin Vulgate (ubera)
readings.en: we will love your breasts more than wine
readings.plain: We will love your breasts more than wine

why: The same question as at 1:2: the consonants allow 'lovemaking' or 'breasts'. The Greek also changes the verb ('love' for 'remember'), so it is a free rendering. The Plain English Translation follows the pointed Hebrew.

a: With good reason they love you
t: With good reason, uprightness, or loved ones
p: The last line has three forms: 'rightly they love you', 'uprightness loves you', and the Qumran scroll's different ending.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.en: rightly they love you
readings.plain: With good reason they love you

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete)
readings.en: uprightness has loved you
readings.plain: Uprightness loves you

readings.w: 6Q6 (6QCant), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook; the words before it are restored
readings.en: upright ones, loved ones (the ending differs from the Masoretic text)
readings.plain: The upright are loved

why: The Hebrew meisharim is used as an adverb elsewhere (Proverbs 23:31; Song 7:9), so 'rightly, with good reason' is a natural reading of the Masoretic text, which the Plain English Translation follows. The Greek takes it as a noun and as the subject.
b: The scroll 6Q6 is broken here, and only the end of the line is preserved, so its reading is uncertain. It is listed because the transcription marks the ending as unlike the Masoretic ahevukha ('they love you'). The editors of 6Q6 are Baillet and others (Discoveries in the Judaean Desert III, 1962).

a: you daughters of Jerusalem
p: Swete's Greek has 'daughters of Israel' here; elsewhere the Greek has 'Jerusalem'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); 6Q6 (6QCant), as transcribed, with a different vowel letter in 'daughters'
readings.en: daughters of Jerusalem
readings.plain: you daughters of Jerusalem

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'daughters of Israel')
readings.en: daughters of Israel
readings.plain: you daughters of Israel

why: Everywhere else the Song says 'daughters of Jerusalem' (2:7; 3:5, 10; 5:8, 16; 8:4), and the Greek has 'Jerusalem' in those places. The Greek 'Israel' at 1:5 stands alone and is probably a slip or a copyist's change, so the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The scroll 6Q6, in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription, writes 'daughters' with a yod where the Masoretic text has a waw; the transcription marks this as a difference in spelling and not in sense. The Greek here is the reading of Swete's Vaticanus text; the critical edition (Rahlfs) is not cited, so the reading is named by the codex and not called 'the Greek'.

a: like a woman wrapped in a veil
t: A veiled woman or a wanderer?
p: The Hebrew word means 'wrapped, veiled'; the Latin Vulgate has 'wander'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'covering herself')
readings.en: like one wrapped in a veil
readings.plain: like a woman wrapped in a veil

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome, vagari, 'to wander')
readings.en: like a wanderer
readings.plain: like a woman who wanders

why: The Hebrew as received makes sense: a veiled woman might be taken for a prostitute (compare Genesis 38:14–15), and she asks why she should wait where she could be mistaken for one. The other reading needs only two letters swapped, and it is old, but the Greek does not support it.
b: Swete's Greek has periballomenē, 'wrapping herself', which agrees with the Masoretic text. The reading 'wander' is the Latin one. Many modern versions choose 'veiled' (Fox, Bloch), while some choose 'wander' (Pope allows it). The Tamar story of Genesis 38:14–15 shows how a veiled woman could be taken for a prostitute by a man who was looking.

a: by the gazelles or by the does of the field
p: The Greek has 'by the powers and by the forces of the field' where the Hebrew has gazelles and does.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); Latin Vulgate (per capreas cervosque camporum, 'by the roes and the harts of the fields')
readings.en: by the gazelles or by the does of the field
readings.plain: by the gazelles or by the does of the field

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete); the same words at 3:5 and, unlike the Hebrew, at 8:4
readings.orig: ἐν δυνάμεσιν καὶ ἐν ἰσχύσεσιν τοῦ ἀγροῦ
readings.en: by the powers and by the forces of the field
readings.plain: by the powers and by the forces of the field

why: The Hebrew words are the names of animals, and the Plain English Translation follows them. They also sound like tseva'ot, 'armies', and the Greek translators seem to have heard that play: they wrote words for 'powers' and 'strengths' and left out the animals.
b: The oath is the same in the Greek at 2:7 and 3:5 (with the article before each noun at 3:5). At 8:4 the Greek again has 'the powers and the forces of the field', although the Hebrew of 8:4 has no gazelles or does (see the note there). The Latin Vulgate keeps the animals.

a: My lover is like a gazelle or a young deer
p: The Greek has 'on the mountains of Bethel' at the end of the comparison.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.orig: דּוֹמֶה דוֹדִי לִצְבִי אוֹ לְעֹפֶר הָאַיָּלִים
readings.en: my lover is like a gazelle or a young deer
readings.plain: My lover is like a gazelle or a young deer

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete)
readings.orig: ὅμοιός ἐστιν ἀδελφιδός μου τῇ δορκάδι ἢ νεβρῷ ἐλάφων ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη Βαιθήλ
readings.en: my lover is like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer on the mountains of Baithel (Bethel)
readings.plain: My lover is like a gazelle or a young deer on the mountains of Bethel

why: The Hebrew of 2:9 has no mountains; the Greek words look like an echo of 2:17, where the Hebrew has 'the mountains of Bether' and the Greek 'mountains of hollows'. The Plain English Translation keeps the shorter Hebrew.
b: The Greek name 'Baithel' (Bethel) at 2:9 probably comes from a confusion with Hebrew Bether in 2:17, whether in the Hebrew the translators had or in the way the Greek was copied. This is the reading of the Vaticanus text as Swete prints it.

a: The blossoms have shown themselves in the land
p: 4QCant-b has two extra words before 'blossoms', as transcribed.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.en: the blossoms have appeared in the land
readings.plain: The blossoms have shown themselves in the land

readings.w: 4QCant-b (4Q107), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook
readings.en: behold, the time of the blossoms has appeared in the land
readings.plain: Look, the time of blossoms has shown itself in the land

why: The scroll's two extra words come from a transcription of a damaged text, and the same scroll adds 'behold' at 2:13. They may be a scribe's echo of 'for behold' in 2:11. The Masoretic text, which agrees with the Greek, is shorter and smoother.
b: The transcription marks the words 'behold' and 'time of' as visible and different from the Masoretic text, with 'the blossoms' restored. The scroll has other small differences in these verses (spelling of 'winter' at 2:11, 'the fig tree' at 2:13); most are spelling. I describe only what the transcription shows. The editor of 4QCant-b is Emanuel Tov, in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert XVI.

a: be like a gazelle or a young deer
t: Does Qumran leave out 'or a young deer'?
p: 4QCant-b, as transcribed, has 'a gazelle' alone here.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'a gazelle or a fawn of the deer')
readings.en: like a gazelle or a young deer
readings.plain: be like a gazelle or a young deer

readings.w: 4QCant-b (4Q107), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook
readings.en: like a gazelle on the mountains of Bether
readings.plain: be like a gazelle

why: The scroll's text is shorter in this transcription, and the loss of 'or a young deer' is probably the scribe's slip or a short form of the line that the other witnesses expand from 2:9 and 8:14. The Plain English Translation keeps the longer Masoretic line, which agrees with the Greek and is in the same words in the two other places.
b: The transcription of 4Q107 here also writes 'dews' (with a tet) where the Masoretic text has 'shadows', which is probably a slip. The scroll is edited by Tov in DJD XVI. In the transcription the word 'on' before 'the mountains of Bether' is restored, not visible on the leather.

a: Who is this coming up out of the wilderness
p: In the transcription, 4QCant-b has 3:5 and then 3:9, with nothing in between.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete); for 3:7–8, also 4QCant-a (4Q106) and 4QCant-c (4Q108)
readings.en: Who is this coming up out of the wilderness (3:6) and the verses to 3:8
readings.plain: Who is this coming up out of the wilderness

readings.w: 4QCant-b (4Q107), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook
readings.orig: … עד שתחפץ // אפריון עשה לו המלך שלמה
readings.en: 3:5 ends, and 3:9 follows at once; there is no 3:6, 3:7 or 3:8
readings.plain: (3:6–8 is not in the scroll)

why: Every other witness has the verses, and the Song's three 'Who is this?' questions (3:6; 6:10; 8:5) need the first. A scribe may have skipped or shortened the text. The fragments are too small to show more.
b: The transcription shows the full text of 3:5 in 4Q107 and then the text of 3:9, most of it restored. 4QCant-a (4Q106) has 3:7–8 but is broken before and after, so it does not show whether it had 3:6. Tov, who edited these scrolls (DJD XVI), is the standard reference for the shorter readings in 4QCant-a and 4QCant-b. They should not be used to argue for a Song that was deliberately shortened at Qumran.

a: daughters of Zion
p: One Qumran scroll has 'daughters of Jerusalem' where the Masoretic text has 'daughters of Zion'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); 4QCant-b (4Q107), as transcribed
readings.en: daughters of Zion
readings.plain: daughters of Zion

readings.w: 4QCant-a (4Q106), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook
readings.en: daughters of Jerusalem
readings.plain: daughters of Jerusalem

why: 'Daughters of Zion' is a rare phrase in the Song (here only) and 'daughters of Jerusalem' is the usual one, so the scroll's reading looks like a scribe's smoothing toward the usual phrase. The Masoretic text, which 4QCant-b shares, is the harder reading. The Plain English Translation follows it.
b: In the transcription 4Q106 shows this word as different from the Masoretic text; the next word in the line is restored, so the reading rests on a few letters. Swete's Greek has no address here at all (it reads 'Go out and look at King Solomon'). In the Song the two phrases name the same chorus.

a: The side of your face behind your veil
t: Temple, or a different word in 4QCant-a?
p: 4QCant-a has a different word where the Masoretic text has 'your temple'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); 4QCant-b (4Q107), as transcribed
readings.en: your temple (the side of your face)
readings.plain: The side of your face behind your veil

readings.w: 4QCant-a (4Q106), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook
readings.en: from your beard or chin (?)
readings.plain: (a word that looks like 'chin', not 'temple')

why: The scroll's word looks like a form of zaqan, 'beard, chin', which does not fit the picture of a pomegranate slice beside the eye. It may be a scribe's slip. If it is not, the sense is unknown.
b: The transcription marks the word as visible and different from the Masoretic text. In 4:2 the same scroll puts 'your teeth' after 'shorn ewes' and writes 'came up' without the relative she-; those differences are also visible in the transcription. I describe only what the transcription shows.

a: Your neck is like David's tower
p: In the transcription, 4QCant-b has 4:3 and then 4:8; 4QCant-a has 4:4–7.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); 4QCant-a (4Q106), as transcribed
readings.en: Your neck is like David's tower (4:4), and the verses to 4:7
readings.plain: Your neck is like David's tower

readings.w: 4QCant-b (4Q107), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook
readings.orig: … מבעד לצמתך // את מן לבנון כלה
readings.en: 4:3 ends and 4:8 follows at once; there is no 4:4–7
readings.plain: (4:4–7 is not in the scroll)

why: 4QCant-a and the other witnesses have these verses. The Plain English Translation keeps the full text.
b: 4Q107 has 4:1–3 and then 4:8–11; 4Q106 has 4:1–7 and then jumps to 6:11 (see the variant at 4:8). The two scrolls therefore leave out different stretches, which is why they are not read as one shortened Song. Tov (DJD XVI) is the standard reference for these shorter readings.

a: With me from Lebanon, bride, / with me from Lebanon, come
p: The Hebrew 'with me' is rendered 'come' in the Greek and Latin.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.orig: אִתִּי מִלְּבָנוֹן כַּלָּה אִתִּי מִלְּבָנוֹן תָּבוֹאִי
readings.en: with me from Lebanon, bride, with me from Lebanon you will come
readings.plain: With me from Lebanon, bride, / with me from Lebanon, come

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'come here'); Latin Vulgate (veni, 'come')
readings.en: come from Lebanon, bride, come from Lebanon
readings.plain: Come from Lebanon, bride. / Come from Lebanon, come

why: The Hebrew itti, 'with me', makes sense and is repeated, and it fits a man who calls her to join him. The Greek and Latin translate as if the word were an imperative 'come' (the same letters can be pointed as the command 'come'). That reading is possible, but the Masoretic reading is the natural one in Hebrew.
b: Most modern English versions follow the Masoretic 'with me'. The imperative reading is old, however, and is behind the 'Veni de Libano' of the Latin liturgy.

a: With me from Lebanon, bride,
p: 4QCant-a has 4:7 and then 6:11, with no text for 4:8 to 6:10.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); 4QCant-b (4Q107) for 4:8–5:1, as transcribed
readings.en: With me from Lebanon, bride (4:8), and the verses to 6:10
readings.plain: With me from Lebanon, bride,

readings.w: 4QCant-a (4Q106), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook
readings.orig: כלך יפה רעיתי ומום אין בך // אל גנת אגוז ירדתי
readings.en: 4:7 ends and 6:11 follows; 4:8 to 6:10 is not in the scroll
readings.plain: (4:8–6:10 is not in the scroll)

why: 4QCant-b has 4:8 to 5:1, so the text is not missing from every copy. A skipped stretch of this length is more likely a scribe's shortening or a broken sheet than a different Song, and the fragments cannot show which.
b: In 4:8 the transcription of 4QCant-b writes 'I will come' (avo'i) where the Masoretic text has tavo'i, 'come', and a different form of the name Amanah (Omnon); these look like spelling or dialect and do not change the sense. The Greek takes Amanah as 'faith' (see the note at 4:8).

a: How lovely your lovemaking is
p: The Greek and Latin read 'your breasts' here, as at 1:2 and 1:4.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.en: how beautiful are your lovemakings
readings.plain: How lovely your lovemaking is

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete); Latin Vulgate (ubera)
readings.orig: מה יפו דדיך → τί ἐκαλλιώθησαν μαστοί σου
readings.en: how beautiful are your breasts
readings.plain: How lovely your breasts are

why: See the variant at 1:2. Here the Hebrew addresses a woman, and the Greek 'your breasts' is possible, but the Masoretic dodayikh is the same word the Song uses of love throughout, and the plain parallel with 'than wine' is the same.
b: The scroll 4QCant-b (4Q107) preserves this verse. In the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription the word is spelled with the same consonants as the Masoretic text, so the scroll cannot decide between 'lovemaking' and 'breasts'.

a: a pool with a lock on it
t: A pool, or a garden again?
p: The Hebrew has 'gal' (a heap or pool); the Greek and the Latin Vulgate have 'garden' a second time.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.en: a heap / pool, locked
readings.plain: a pool with a lock on it

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'a garden shut up'); Latin Vulgate (hortus conclusus again)
readings.en: a garden, locked
readings.plain: a garden with a lock on it

why: The Hebrew gal is normally 'a heap' (of stones) or 'a wave'. The sense 'a pool' or 'spring' is a guess from the parallel 'spring'. The Greek and Latin repeat 'garden'. Since 'garden' and 'heap' differ by one letter (nun and lamed), 'garden' may be a scribe's easing; the Plain English Translation follows the harder Hebrew word.
b: The three images are 'garden', 'spring/pool' and 'fountain', and the two readings keep the same sense of an enclosed source of life.

a: I have eaten my honeycomb and my honey. / I have drunk my wine and my milk.
p: The Septuagint has 'bread' for 'honeycomb', and 4QCant-b puts the drinking line before the eating line.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.orig: אָכַלְתִּי יַעְרִי עִם דִּבְשִׁי שָׁתִיתִי יֵינִי עִם חֲלָבִי
readings.en: I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk
readings.plain: I have eaten my honeycomb and my honey. / I have drunk my wine and my milk.

readings.w: 4QCant-b (4Q107), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (the two lines in the other order)
readings.orig: שתיתי יין עם חלבי אכלתי יערי עם דבשי
readings.en: I have drunk my wine with my milk, I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey
readings.plain: I have drunk my wine and my milk. / I have eaten my honeycomb and my honey.

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'my bread with my honey')
readings.orig: ἔφαγον ἄρτον μου μετὰ μέλιτός μου, ἔπιον οἶνόν μου μετὰ γάλακτός μου
readings.en: I have eaten my bread with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk
readings.plain: I have eaten my bread and my honey. / I have drunk my wine and my milk.

why: The Masoretic order and wording are the oldest in Hebrew that we have complete. The scroll differs only in the order of two lines, which does not change the meaning, and the Greek 'bread' looks like a translator's easing of the rare word ya'ar (honeycomb), which appears also in 1 Samuel 14:25–27.
b: In the transcription, 4Q107 also writes the line about myrrh and spice as the Masoretic text does and reverses only the next two. The scroll is damaged, and the transposition is the transcription's reading, not a restored guess. The edition is Tov's in DJD XVI.

a: Eat, friends! Drink, and be drunk with lovemaking!
t: Be drunk with lovemaking, or 'O lovers'?
p: The last word can be 'lovemaking' or a call to 'lovers'; the Greek has 'brothers'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex), dodim read as 'lovemaking'
readings.en: drink and be drunk with love
readings.plain: Eat, friends! Drink, and be drunk with lovemaking!

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'brothers'); many modern versions ('lovers')
readings.orig: φάγετε, πλησίοι, καὶ πίετε καὶ μεθύσθητε, ἀδελφοί
readings.en: eat, neighbors, and drink and get drunk, brothers
readings.plain: Eat, friends! Drink, and be drunk, O lovers!

why: Dodim is the Song's word for lovemaking (1:2, 4; 4:10; 7:12), and the line parallels 'drink and be drunk' with an object. The vocative 'O lovers' is a possible reading of the same word, and the Greek 'brothers' takes it that way. The Plain English Translation keeps 'lovemaking' because of the Song's usage; the choice is close.
b: The same consonants are read either way. Which reading one chooses also fixes the voice that speaks: with 'O lovers' it is a call to the friends; with 'lovemaking' it is a toast to the couple.

a: like towers of sweet herbs
t: Towers of herbs or plants yielding perfume?
p: The Hebrew has 'towers'; the Greek reads a verb: 'producing perfumes'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex), migdelot
readings.en: towers of aromatic herbs
readings.plain: like towers of sweet herbs

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'producing perfumes')
readings.en: growing / yielding perfumes
readings.plain: growing sweet herbs

why: The same letters can be pointed 'towers' (migdelot) or 'making to grow' (magdilot). The Masoretic pointing gives a picture of banks of spice that stand up like towers, a fit with the garden bed in the line before it. The Greek has the participle. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic text; both give the sense of strong perfume rising from his cheeks.

a: among the chariots of my noble people
p: The Greek and Latin read a name, 'Aminadab'; the Hebrew words are 'ammi nadiv'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex: two words joined by a hyphen; Aleppo Codex: two words)
readings.en: my people, a noble / my noble people
readings.plain: among the chariots of my noble people

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'chariots of Aminadab'); Latin Vulgate (quadrigae Aminadab)
readings.en: the chariots of Amminadab (Amminadib)
readings.plain: among the chariots of Amminadib

why: Both readings use the same letters and differ in how they are divided. The Leningrad Codex joins the two words with a hyphen, the Aleppo Codex writes them apart, and the word list marks a variant that writes the single name Aminadav. The name 'Amminadab' is well known (Exodus 6:23; Ruth 4:19), but nothing in the Song says who he is or why his chariots matter. The Plain English Translation follows the two-word Hebrew and treats the name as a possible reading.
b: 'Noble' (nadiv) is also used of princes (Psalm 47:9). If 'nadib' is a name, the passage may refer to a figure who was famous in popular memory but is now unknown, or to a place; the Greek and Latin took it as a person. Modern versions are split.

a: Come back, come back, Shulammite! / Come back, come back, so that we may look at you.
p: The Qumran scroll 4QCant-a, as transcribed, has only one pair of 'come back' before 'that we may look at you'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex); Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'return, return' twice)
readings.orig: שׁוּבִי שׁוּבִי הַשּׁוּלַמִּית שׁוּבִי שׁוּבִי וְנֶחֱזֶה בָּךְ
readings.en: come back, come back, Shulammite, come back, come back, that we may look at you
readings.plain: Come back, come back, Shulammite! / Come back, come back, so that we may look at you.

readings.w: 4QCant-a (4Q106), Qumran, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook
readings.en: come back, come back, Shulammite, that we may look at you
readings.plain: Come back, come back, Shulammite, so that we may look at you.

why: The longer text is attested in all the other witnesses. The scroll's shorter line may come from a scribe's eye jumping from the first pair of 'shuvi' to the second ('haplography'), or it may be an older form of the line that the longer text expanded. This is one of the readings in which a Qumran scroll is shorter than the Masoretic text (Tov).
b: Emanuel Tov, who edited the Song scrolls (DJD XVI), is the standard reference for the places where 4QCant-a and 4QCant-b are shorter than the Masoretic text. The fragments are small and the places where they differ are few, so they cannot show that a shorter Song was the norm at Qumran.

a: gliding over the lips of sleepers
p: The Hebrew has 'the lips of sleepers'; the Greek and the Latin have 'lips and teeth'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex), yeshenim
readings.en: gliding over the lips of sleepers
readings.plain: gliding over the lips of sleepers

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'my lips and teeth'); Latin Vulgate (labiis et dentibus, 'lips and teeth')
readings.orig: שִׂפְתֵי שִׁנַּיִם → χείλεσίν μου καὶ ὀδοῦσιν
readings.en: flowing over my lips and teeth
readings.plain: gliding over lips and teeth

why: The Hebrew yeshenim ('sleepers') and shinnayim ('teeth') are close, and a tradition of reading 'lips and teeth' is very old. The Masoretic text is the harder reading and has a sense: wine that is so smooth it moves the lips even of sleeping men (or men asleep from wine). The Greek is a smoother text. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The word dovev is also uncertain: 'gliding' or 'moving' or 'making to speak' (Proverbs and Job use a related form); the meaning 'make the lips of sleepers move' has been taken as wine that loosens even sleeping tongues. The rabbis took the lips of sleepers as the dead, whose lips move when a scholar's teaching is quoted in their name (Bavli Yevamot 97a).

a: I belong to my lover, / and his desire is toward me
p: The Greek reads 'his turning toward me' where the Hebrew has 'his desire'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.en: I am my lover's, and on me is his desire
readings.plain: I belong to my lover, / and his desire is toward me

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'and his turning is toward me')
readings.en: and his return / turning is toward me
readings.plain: I belong to my lover, / and his turning is toward me

why: The Greek word epistrophē ('turning back') might render Hebrew teshuvah, 'return'. The two Hebrew words differ by a few letters. The Masoretic reading is rare and fits the three-way echo of Genesis 3:16 and 4:7. The Greek translator may have read a more usual word, or tried to ease a hard one.
b: In Genesis 3:16 and 4:7 the Greek uses apostrophē, 'turning away', for the same Hebrew word, so the Greek of the Song and of Genesis agree in translating teshuqah as a kind of 'turning'.

a: and you would teach me
p: The Greek has no 'teach me' and says 'into the room of her who conceived me' as at 3:4.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex), telammedeni
readings.en: you would teach me (or: she who taught me)
readings.plain: and you would teach me

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete): no 'teach me'; 'and into the room of her who conceived me'
readings.orig: καὶ εἰς ταμεῖον τῆς συλλαβούσης με
readings.en: and into the room of the one who conceived me
readings.plain: and to the room of the woman who conceived me

why: The Hebrew form can be read 'you will teach me' (second person) or 'she will teach me' (the mother, third person), and some read it as 'she who taught me', so it is itself unclear. The Greek has a clean parallel with 3:4, and may be a translator's assimilation; or it may reflect a Hebrew with heder horati that the Masoretic text lost. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.
b: Whom does she imagine as teacher? If 'you', it is the lover who teaches her love, and the verse gives the Song its image of a woman learning from a man. If 'she', it is her mother, who taught her what a bride should know. Jewish readers have found Israel taught by God; Christian readers, the Church taught by Christ.

a: leaning on her lover
p: The Greek has two words: 'made white' and 'leaning'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex)
readings.en: leaning on her lover
readings.plain: leaning on her lover

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'made white, leaning on her lover')
readings.orig: λελευκαθισμένη, ἐπιστηριζομένη ἐπὶ τὸν ἀδελφιδὸν αὐτῆς
readings.en: dressed in white, leaning on her lover
readings.plain: dressed in white, leaning on her lover

why: The Hebrew has one rare word. The Greek renders it twice, 'made white' and 'leaning', which looks like a translator's double guess at a rare word. The Latin Vulgate has a different guess, 'overflowing with delights' (deliciis affluens). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

a: Under the apple tree I woke you.
p: The Hebrew letters can be read 'I woke you' to a man or to a woman.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex), pointed as masculine (orartikha)
readings.en: I woke you (a man); so the woman speaks
readings.plain: Under the apple tree I woke you.

readings.w: The same consonants read as feminine (orartikh), a possible reading of the unpointed text
readings.en: I woke you (a woman); so the man speaks
readings.plain: Under the apple tree I woke you.

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: exēgeirā se); Latin Vulgate (suscitavi te)
readings.en: I woke you (the pronoun does not show the gender)
readings.plain: Under the apple tree I woke you.

why: The pointing is the old tradition of reading, and the line that follows ('your mother went into labor with you') has the same masculine ending. The English 'you' shows no gender, so the Plain English Translation reads the same either way; the difference is who is speaking, and the note at 8:5 gives the views.
b: The consonants of the verb and of 'your mother' end in the same letter for 'you' masculine and 'you' feminine; only the vowel marks decide. The Greek and Latin pronouns are the same for both genders, so they do not settle the question.

a: a flame of Yah
p: The Hebrew has one word with the ending 'Yah'; the Greek and Latin have no name of God.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, Aleppo Codex): one word, shalhevetyah
readings.en: a flame of Yah / a mighty flame
readings.plain: a flame of Yah

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete: 'its flames')
readings.en: its flames
readings.plain: its flames

why: The Hebrew word is rare and reads naturally as a noun plus the divine name Yah, as the Masoretic accents show. The Greek has 'its flames' (phloges autēs), which fits a Hebrew without the ending, and so may be a smoother text or a different one. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and gives the superlative reading in the notes.
b: The Latin Vulgate also lacks the divine name: lampades ignis atque flammarum, 'lamps of fire and of flames'. The shortness of the Greek is one reason that some scholars hold the name to be a later addition. The Masoretic reading is the best attested in Hebrew.
